questions.question: Maya spun a fair spinner with 4 equal sections (red, blue, green, yellow) 20 times and wrote the results in a table: red 4, blue 7, green 5, yellow 4. The theoretical probability of blue is 1/4, so about 5 blues were expected. Which statement best compares the results with the expectation?
options: Blue came up 7 times instead of about 5, and a small gap like that is normal in only 20 spins.
Blue really is more likely than the other colours, because blue won in these 20 spins.
The spinner must be broken, because a fair spinner has to land on blue exactly 5 times in 20 spins.
The theoretical probability of blue must be changed to 7/20, because that is what the table shows.
questions.explain: Compare the experimental result 7 out of 20 with the theoretical expectation 5 out of 20 (that is 1/4): they are close, and a gap of 2 is ordinary chance variation. The common trap is the idea that a fair spinner must land on blue exactly 5 times.

questions.question: Owen flipped a fair coin 10 times and filled in a table: heads 6, tails 4. The theoretical probability of heads is 1/2, so 5 heads were expected. Which comparison is correct?
options: Owen must have miscounted, because 10 flips of a fair coin always give 5 heads.
The experimental probability of heads is 6/10 and the theoretical is 5/10, so the experiment came out a little higher, which often happens in only 10 flips.
The coin is unfair, because heads beat tails in these 10 flips.
The theoretical probability of heads is now 6/10, since that is the result Owen got.
questions.explain: Line the two numbers up: experimental 6/10 against theoretical 5/10, so the difference is just one extra head. Watch out for the idea that a fair coin has to give exactly 5 heads in 10 flips — real experiments wobble around the expected value.

questions.question: A table records 25 spins of a fair spinner with 5 equal sections, one of them a star. The table shows star 4 times and 'not star' 21 times. The theoretical probability of a star is 1/5, so 5 stars were expected. What is the best explanation of the difference?
options: Something is wrong with the spinner, because a 1/5 chance means the star has to show up exactly 5 times in 25 spins.
The star is truly less likely than 1/5, and these 25 spins prove it.
Getting 4 stars is one below the 5 expected, and experimental results can sit near the theoretical value without matching it.
The theoretical probability of the star should be rewritten as 4/25.
questions.explain: Expected stars = 1/5 of 25 = 5, and the experiment gave 4, so the difference is only 1. The trap is treating any gap as proof of a problem — 25 spins is nowhere near enough to overturn the theoretical 1/5.

questions.question: Priya rolled a fair six-sided die 30 times and made a table of the results. It shows that 6 came up 3 times. The theoretical probability of rolling a 6 is 1/6, so 5 sixes were expected. Which statement best describes the difference?
options: The die is loaded against 6, because 3 is less than the 5 that were expected.
There is nothing to explain, because 3 out of 30 is the same as 1 out of 6.
Priya must have written the rolls down wrong, because 30 rolls of a fair die must give exactly 5 sixes.
The experimental probability of 6 is 3/30, which is 1/10, a bit below the theoretical 1/6, and a gap like that is expected in only 30 rolls.
questions.explain: Write the experimental probability as 3/30 = 1/10 and compare it with the theoretical 1/6 (which would be 5 sixes); they are close but not equal, and that is normal. Two traps: thinking 3/30 equals 1/6, and thinking a fair die owes you exactly 5 sixes.

questions.question: For a fair number cube, the theoretical probability of rolling a 4 is 1/6. In which experiment would you expect the experimental probability of rolling a 4 to land closest to 1/6?
options: 600 rolls, because the experimental probability gets closer to the theoretical probability as the number of trials grows.
12 rolls, because 12 is double 6, so the results come out exactly 2 fours.
6 rolls, because there are 6 faces on the cube.
20 rolls, because after 20 trials you can already tell whether the cube is fair.
questions.explain: More trials smooth out the wobble, so the experimental probability drifts toward the theoretical 1/6 as the number of rolls grows. Matching the number of trials to the number of faces does not force the result, and a handful of trials is never enough to judge a cube.

questions.question: At a school fair in Kelowna, a prize wheel is built so the theoretical probability of winning is 1/4. Sofia takes 40 spins and wins 12 times. Which is the best comparison of her results with the expectation?
options: The wheel is set to hand out extra prizes, because 12 is more than 10.
The experimental probability 12/40 = 3/10 is a little above the theoretical 1/4 (10 wins out of 40), and being 2 wins over is ordinary chance variation.
The organizers made a mistake, because 1/4 of 40 has to give exactly 10 wins.
Since the results differ, the true probability of winning is really 3/10.
questions.explain: Find the expected wins first: 1/4 of 40 = 10, then compare with the 12 that actually happened. A difference of 2 in 40 spins does not change the theoretical 1/4, and it does not prove the wheel was tampered with.

questions.question: A spinner has a theoretical probability of 2/5 of landing on green. A class plans to spin it 200 times. Which statement shows the best reasoning about what will happen?
options: Exactly 80 spins will be green, because 2/5 of 200 is 80.
The class can decide the spinner is fair after only 5 spins, since 2 of those 5 should be green.
About 80 spins should be green, and the actual count will probably land near 80 without being exactly 80.
The number of greens cannot be predicted at all, because experiments are random.
questions.explain: Theoretical probability predicts roughly 2/5 of 200 = 80 greens, so 'about 80' is the right kind of claim. The usual trap is demanding the experiment hit 80 exactly; the opposite trap is deciding from 5 spins, which is far too few.

questions.question: The theoretical probability of heads is 1/2. Group A flips a coin 20 times and gets 13 heads (13/20 = 0.65). Group B flips 200 times and gets 106 heads (106/200 = 0.53). Whose experimental probability is closer to the theoretical one, and why?
options: Group A, because 13 heads out of 20 shows the coin favours heads.
Group A, because it is easier to land near 1/2 when there are fewer flips.
Neither, because neither group got exactly half heads, so both experiments failed.
Group B, because 0.53 is nearer to 0.5 than 0.65 is, and more trials usually pull the experimental probability closer to the theoretical.
questions.explain: Turn both records into numbers and measure the gap from 0.5: Group A is off by 0.15 while Group B is off by only 0.03. Fewer flips make big gaps easier, not harder, and no group needs to hit exactly half to count as a success.

questions.question: Jae flips a loonie 4 times and gets 3 heads. He tells his friend the loonie is unfair. Remember two things: the theoretical probability of heads is 1/2, and Jae did only 4 flips. What is the best response to Jae?
options: He is wrong: 4 flips is far too few to judge; he should flip many more times and see if the results settle near 1/2.
He is right: a fair loonie must give exactly 2 heads in 4 flips, so getting 3 heads shows the loonie is not fair.
He is wrong: flipping can never be used to judge a coin, because experimental results say nothing about whether it is fair.
He is right: 3 out of 4 is much more than half, so 4 flips are already enough to show the loonie favours heads.
questions.explain: With only 4 flips, results like 3 heads happen easily by chance, so they cannot show the coin is unfair — many more trials are needed before the experimental probability means anything. Experimental data is still useful for judging a coin; it just has to come from a lot of trials.

questions.question: Ms. Chen's class tests a spinner with 8 equal sections, one marked WIN, so the theoretical probability of a win is 1/8. Group 1 spins 16 times and wins 4 times (4/16 = 1/4). Then the whole class pools its data: 400 spins with 46 wins, while 1/8 of 400 would be 50. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: The spinner really wins 1/4 of the time, because that is what Group 1 measured, and real spins beat the 1/8 on paper.
46 wins out of 400 is close to the 50 expected, so the spinner looks fair, and Group 1's 1/4 came from too few spins.
The spinner is broken, because 1/8 of 400 is 50 and a fair spinner must give exactly 50 wins, not 46, in 400 spins.
Group 1's result and the class result cannot be compared, because 16 spins and 400 spins are different sizes of experiment.
questions.explain: Compare each set with its own expectation: 1/8 of 400 = 50 versus 46 actual is a tiny gap, while 4 out of 16 is a big gap built on very few spins. Small samples swing wildly, and a difference of 4 wins in 400 spins is not evidence of a broken spinner.

questions.question: A gift shop on the BC Ferries sells mystery keychain boxes and claims that 1 of every 5 boxes holds a rare orca keychain. Liam buys 15 boxes and finds 2 orcas. Which statement compares his result with the theoretical expectation correctly?
options: About 3 orcas were expected (1/5 of 15) and he found 2; a true 1-in-5 claim must give exactly 3, so the claim is false.
Only 2 orcas turned up in his 15 boxes, and 15 boxes is plenty to test with, so the shop's 1-in-5 claim must be false.
About 3 orcas were expected (1/5 of 15) and he found 2; one under is a small, ordinary gap, so the 1-in-5 claim still looks fine.
His experimental probability of 2/15 replaces the theoretical 1/5, because real boxes beat a claim, so the chance is now 2/15.
questions.explain: First find the expectation, 1/5 of 15 = 3, then compare it with the 2 he actually found; a difference of 1 out of 15 boxes is exactly the kind of wobble experiments produce. An experimental result does not overwrite the theoretical probability, and 15 boxes is far too few to call the claim false.

questions.question: A fair spinner has 10 equal sections numbered 1 to 10, so the theoretical probability of landing on 7 is 1/10. In 50 spins, the number 7 comes up 8 times, while 5 sevens were expected. Ana says the spinner is rigged for 7. Ben says a fair spinner should have given exactly 5 sevens. Who is right?
options: Ana is right: 8 sevens out of 50 is well above the 5 expected, and 50 spins is enough to prove the spinner favours 7.
Ben is right: 1/10 of 50 is 5, and a fair spinner must produce exactly that number, so anything else shows a problem.
Both are right: a difference of 3 shows something is definitely wrong, so the spinner is rigged and also not fair.
Neither is right: 8 sevens is a bit above the 5 expected, which happens easily in 50 spins, so more spins are needed.
questions.explain: The experimental probability 8/50 sits a little above the theoretical 1/10 (5 out of 50), and a gap of 3 spins is well within normal chance variation. Two traps meet here: calling a spinner rigged from a short run, and demanding the experiment match the expected count exactly.
